title: Managing Your Team with Copilot — Tasks, Blockers & Workload

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Managing a team means constantly tracking three things: what everyone is working on, what's blocking progress, and whether the workload is balanced. Without tooling, this happens through a chain of status meetings, email check-ins, and ad hoc conversations — each consuming time that could be spent actually doing the work.

With Copilot connected to your task management system (Jira, Azure DevOps, GitHub Issues), you can get a complete picture of your team's status in minutes — not meetings. You can identify blockers before they become crises, reallocate work intelligently, and produce reports for your own manager without manually gathering information.

You'll learn:
- Morning team status: automated briefing from your task system
- Identifying blockers and at-risk deliverables
- Work distribution and reallocation analysis
- Status reports generated directly from task data
- How to ask each team member the right questions via Copilot-drafted check-ins
- Tracking deliverables without micromanaging

## The Morning Team Briefing

Instead of starting your day with a status meeting, start it with a Copilot briefing that answers the same questions in 2 minutes.

**Azure DevOps version (Copilot Agent Mode with ADO MCP):**
```
Search our Azure DevOps project for all work items assigned to my team members.
For each team member [list names or tag the team], show:
1. What they have In Progress
2. What they have in their To Do queue
3. Anything marked as Blocked or at risk
4. Anything past its due date

Highlight any items that have been In Progress for more than [X] days 
without a status update — these need a check-in.
```

**Jira version:**
```
Search Jira for all issues in project [PROJECT-KEY] assigned to team members 
[list names]. Group by assignee. For each person show:
- In Progress items with days since last update
- Blocked items with the blocker noted
- Overdue items (due date passed, not resolved)
- Upcoming items due this week
Flag anyone with zero active in-progress items — they may need new work assigned.
```

**GitHub Issues version:**
```
Using the GitHub MCP server, list all open issues assigned to team members 
in repository [repo-name]. Group by assignee. Flag: items with no activity 
in the last 7 days, items past milestone, items labeled 'blocked'.
```

Run this every morning before your team standup. You walk into the meeting knowing what to ask about, not discovering it live.

## Identifying Blockers Before They Become Crises

Blockers are most expensive when they're discovered late. Copilot can proactively surface them.

### Blocker Detection Prompt

```
Search all In Progress work items in [project] for the last 14 days.
For each item that has been In Progress for more than 5 days without moving:
1. What is the item?
2. Who is it assigned to?
3. When was it last updated?
4. Are there any comments indicating why it hasn't moved?
5. What is the impact if this item is delayed further?

Rank these by business impact (use priority field and sprint/milestone assignment 
as proxies). Show the top 5 most at-risk items.
```

### Dependency Analysis

```
For the items due this sprint/iteration:
- Which items are blocked by other items not yet complete?
- Which items have external dependencies (other teams, approvals, data from vendors)?
- If the top 3 blockers aren't resolved by [date], which deliverables are at risk?

Create a simple dependency risk table: Item | Blocker | Owner of Blocker | Risk if Unresolved.
```

### Automatic Blocker Escalation

For blockers that persist more than 3 days:
```
An item has been blocked for [N] days: [item details, blocker description].
Draft an escalation message to [relevant person/team] that:
1. States what's blocked and for how long
2. Explains what we need from them specifically
3. States the impact on our delivery if this isn't resolved by [date]
4. Proposes a specific meeting time if a conversation is needed

Tone: collaborative, not accusatory. Focus on the shared goal, not the blame.
```

## Workload Analysis and Reallocation

One of the most valuable management tasks Copilot can assist with is workload balancing — ensuring no one is overloaded while others have capacity.

### Current Workload Snapshot

```
For each team member [list names], find all their In Progress and To Do items 
for this sprint. Estimate the total workload:
- Count of active items
- Story points (if tracked) or priority-weighted count
- Any items marked High or Critical priority

Identify: who appears overloaded (5+ active items or 20+ story points) 
and who has capacity (fewer than 2 active items).
```

### Reallocation Suggestions

```
[Name] is overloaded with [X items]. [Other name] has capacity.
Look at [overloaded person]'s queue and identify work items that could be 
reassigned without requiring specialized knowledge. 
For each transferable item: explain why it's transferable and what the 
handoff would need to include.
```

### Sprint Velocity Tracking

```
Compare our last 3 completed sprints:
- How many story points were planned vs. completed?
- Which types of work (bug/feature/tech-debt) had the best completion rate?
- Which team members had the highest completion rates?
- What patterns explain the discrepancies?

Based on this history, what is a realistic commitment for the next sprint?
```

## Delegating Work via Copilot-Drafted Task Assignments

When delegating work, clarity prevents the 'I wasn't sure what you wanted' problem. Copilot can help you write task descriptions that leave no room for ambiguity.

### Creating Clear Task Descriptions

```
Create a task ticket in [Jira/ADO] for [team member name].

Task: [what needs to be done]
Context: [why this task exists and how it fits the bigger picture]
Definition of Done: [exactly what 'complete' looks like — specific, measurable]
Resources: [links, files, people to consult]
Deadline: [date and why this date]
Estimated effort: [your rough estimate]
Questions to answer before starting: [anything ambiguous they should clarify first]

Write the description as if the assignee knows the project but has never 
seen this specific task before. Do not assume context that isn't written down.
```

### Bulk Task Creation for Projects

```
I'm planning a new work initiative: [project description].
Break this into discrete tasks for assignment. For each task:
- Title (short, action-verb format)
- Description (what exactly needs to be done)
- Who this is appropriate for (based on skill level: junior/senior/specialist)
- Dependencies (what must be done first)
- Estimated effort (Small/Medium/Large)

Create these as a structured list I can review before creating tickets in [ADO/Jira].
```

## Status Reports to Your Manager

One of the most time-consuming tasks for a team leader: writing status reports upward. Copilot can generate these directly from your task system data.

### Weekly Status Report from Task Data

```
Using the [ADO/Jira] MCP, pull data for our team's sprint or current period.

Generate a weekly status report for my manager with these sections:

## This Week
- Work completed: [list completed items with brief description]
- Work in progress: [items underway with expected completion]
- Issues/risks: [blockers, delays, resource issues]

## Next Week
- Planned work: [items starting next week]
- Decisions needed: [anything I need from leadership]

## Metrics
- Items completed vs. planned: [count]
- Any items carried over and why

Tone: concise, factual. My manager doesn't need implementation details — 
they need to know if we're on track and what they need to do.
Length: under 400 words.
```

### Sprint/Milestone Completion Report

```
Pull all completed items from the last sprint in [project].
Generate a sprint completion report:
1. Planned vs. actual completion (count and story points)
2. Highlights — the most significant things we delivered
3. What didn't get done and why (factual, not defensive)
4. Key decisions made during the sprint
5. Recommendations for next sprint based on this sprint's outcomes

Format as a brief email I can send to project stakeholders.
```

sections.title: Run Your First Automated Team Briefing
sections.content:
Generate a complete team status picture without opening your task management tool.

**Prerequisites:** ADO or Jira MCP configured (from lesson 6-17). If not yet set up, complete the MCP setup first.

**Step 1 — Run the morning briefing prompt:**
```
Search [your project] for all open work items assigned to [your team members — list names or team group].
Group by assignee. For each person:
- What are they working on right now (In Progress)?
- What's next in their queue?
- Anything blocked or overdue?

After the per-person summary, give me a team-level view:
- How many items are actively in progress across the team?
- Are there any shared blockers affecting multiple people?
- Does anyone appear to have no active work?
```

**Step 2 — Blocker check:**
```
From the items above, which have been In Progress the longest? 
Any item In Progress for more than 7 days without a comment or status change 
is a potential invisible blocker. List them.
```

**Step 3 — Compare to your mental model.**
Before running these prompts, write down what you expected to see. After seeing the output: was anything surprising? Anything you forgot was assigned to someone? Any blocker you didn't know about?

**Step 4 — Draft one check-in message** for the most at-risk item:
```
Draft a brief, friendly check-in message to [team member] about [item].
I want to know: current status, any blockers, expected completion.
Tone: supportive manager checking in, not micromanager demanding accountability.
Length: 3-4 sentences. This will be sent as a Slack message or Teams chat.
```

**Outcome:** A complete team status picture in under 10 minutes — the same information you'd normally get from a 30-minute standup.

sections.title: Workshop A — Write a Delegation That Gets Results
sections.content:
Practice writing task descriptions that prevent the 'I wasn't sure what you wanted' problem.

**Step 1 — Think of a real task** you need to delegate to a team member this week.

**Step 2 — Draft the task description using Copilot:**
```
Help me write a task delegation description for a team member.

Task: [what needs to be done — your rough description]
Assignee: [their role/level, not name]
Context: [why this task exists]
What done looks like: [your current sense of completion criteria]

Please:
1. Rewrite the task title in clear action-verb format
2. Write a description that assumes they know the project but not this specific task
3. Add explicit Definition of Done with measurable criteria
4. Identify any questions they might have that aren't answered — list them for me to fill in
```

**Step 3 — Fill in the gaps** Copilot identified.

**Step 4 — The delegation test:** Read the description as if you're the assignee seeing it for the first time. Could you start work without asking any questions? If you'd need to ask something, add the answer.

**Step 5 — Create the actual ticket** in your task management system.

**Step 6 — After the task is complete, evaluate:** Did the assignee ask clarifying questions that should have been in the brief? Were there any 'that's not what I meant' moments? Use these to improve your next delegation brief.

**The goal:** Zero clarification questions after you delegate. Every time someone has to ask a clarifying question, it's a gap in the brief — not a gap in their ability.

sections.title: Workshop B — Generate a Status Report from Task Data
sections.content:
Generate a real upward status report directly from your project management system.

**Step 1 — Connect to your task system** (Jira/ADO/GitHub MCP).

**Step 2 — Pull the data:**
```
For [project/sprint/current period]:
- List all completed items with their titles
- List all in-progress items with expected completion
- List any items that were planned but not started
- List any items that are blocked with the blocker description
- Show total story points or item counts planned vs. completed
```

**Step 3 — Generate the report:**
```
Using the data above, write a weekly status report for my manager.
They care about: are we on track? Is anything at risk? What do they need to decide?

Format:
**[Project name] — Week [X] Status**

**On Track / At Risk / Off Track** (pick one, bold it)

**Completed this week:** [bulleted list]
**In progress:** [bulleted list with expected completion]
**Risks/issues:** [any blocks or delays]
**Decisions needed from leadership:** [explicit ask if any]

Length: scannable in 60 seconds. No filler.
```

**Step 4 — Switch to Claude** and refine:
```
Review this status report for tone and clarity. My manager is busy and direct.
Flag anything that's vague, passive, or that buries important information.
Suggest specific improvements.
```

**Step 5 — Send it.** Or if it's not a real report, compare it to what you would have written manually. What's different? What's better? What's missing?

sections.title: Workshop C — Build a Team Dashboard Prompt System
sections.content:
Create a reusable prompt system that generates your key management views on demand.

**Create `~/.copilot/prompts/team-management/` and add these prompt files:**

**`team-morning-briefing.prompt.md`** — Your daily team status pull. Fill in team member names and project key.

**`team-blocker-check.prompt.md`** — Deep dive on everything stalled or at risk.

**`team-workload-balance.prompt.md`** — Workload distribution across team members with reallocation suggestions.

**`team-status-report.prompt.md`** — Weekly upward report in your manager's preferred format.

**`team-sprint-review.prompt.md`** — End-of-sprint retrospective data pull and summary.

**For each prompt file, customize:**
- Your team members' names or identifiers
- Your project key (PROJ-123 or ADO project name)
- Your manager's preferences (length, format, what they care about)
- Your sprint/iteration cadence

**Test each prompt** with real data from your task system. Refine the format until the output is immediately usable.

**Create a master `team-dashboard.prompt.md`** that runs all five in sequence:
```markdown
Run the following team management checks in sequence:
1. Morning briefing — overall team status
2. Blocker check — anything stalled
3. Workload balance — anyone over/underloaded
4. Flag any items I should personally address today

Give me the most important action from each section — one thing I should do
before my standup this morning.
```

**Outcome:** A personal management dashboard that takes your team's raw task data and turns it into a prioritized action list — every morning, in 3 minutes.

sections.question: You run the morning team briefing and discover one team member has 8 items In Progress and no items completed in 7 days. What should Copilot help you do next?
options: Immediately reassign all their work to other team members
Use Copilot to identify which of their items are most at risk, draft a supportive check-in message asking about status and any blockers, and analyze whether any items can be removed from their plate
Mark all their in-progress items as blocked in the system
Generate a performance report and escalate to HR
sections.explanation: 8 items In Progress with no completions in 7 days is a signal — but not a conclusion. The right response is investigation, not escalation. Use Copilot to: (1) find which items are highest priority and most at risk, (2) draft a check-in message asking for status and whether anything is blocked or unclear, (3) identify if any items can be deprioritized or reassigned to reduce the load. Most blockers are systemic (unclear requirements, waiting for others, unexpected complexity) not performance issues. The briefing gives you the signal — Copilot helps you investigate and respond appropriately.

sections.question: You want to create 15 task tickets in Azure DevOps for a new project using Copilot. What is the safest workflow?
options: Ask Copilot to create all 15 tickets at once using the ADO MCP tools
Ask Copilot to first generate a structured list of all 15 tasks for your review, then create them one batch at a time after you've verified the titles, descriptions, and assignments
Create the tickets manually — Copilot is not reliable enough for ticket creation
Ask Copilot to create them one at a time so you can verify each before the next
sections.explanation: Bulk ticket creation is powerful but needs a review step. The safest pattern: (1) ask Copilot to generate the full list as text first, (2) review all 15 in one pass — checking titles, descriptions, assignments, and sequencing, (3) ask Copilot to make corrections to the list, (4) then create the tickets in batches of 3-5. Creating all 15 at once without review risks tickets with wrong assignments, unclear descriptions, or missing dependencies that are harder to fix after creation. The structured list review step costs 5 minutes and prevents hours of cleanup.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-24 complete.** Managing a team with Copilot shifts your role from information collector to decision maker — the task system pulls the data, Copilot synthesizes it, and you spend your time on the decisions that require human judgment. The morning briefing, blocker detection, and workload analysis prompts together replace most routine check-in meetings with a 10-minute data pull. Lesson 6-25 covers Meetings — agenda preparation, real-time note support, action item extraction, and follow-up automation.
